extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys/prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples applying the USPTO 2014 IEG/Alice-Mayo two-step analysis to determine §101 patent eligibility, showing how to identify judicial exceptions and when additional claim elements do (or do not) amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). (Step 1: YES/NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a series of acts = a process (statutory category). Note that the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim may cover performance by hand or by a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical relationships and algorithms (e.g., specific formulas) have been characterized as abstract ideas or laws of nature by the courts (citations: Mackay Radio, Flook, etc.). Point to the claim elements (e.g., generating/scaling steps, formulas) that recite the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: additional limitations must amount to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the exception (Step 2B: YES/NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider each additional element alone and the claim elements as an ordered combination. Generic computer implementation or merely adding conventional activities ordinarily does not amount to significantly more; a specific application that improves technology or effects a transformation can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble limiting effect — 'life, meaning and vitality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the preamble gives 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim such that it limits the claim scope (if so, treat preamble limitations as claim limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preamble only states purpose or field of use it does not limit the claim. See MPEP 2111.02 for guidance on when preamble language is limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting that a claim is 'computer-implemented' or adding generic computer components does not by itself qualify as significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere recitation of 'computer-implemented' is akin to adding the words 'apply it' and is not enough. Generic components performing generic functions (accessing a database, performing calculations, outputting a result) described at a high level of generality are well-understood, routine and conventional and do not add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting use to a particular technological environment is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply restricting the abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., graphical user interface) is not typically enough to make the claim significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found that merely limiting the use of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (see Flook) does not supply significantly more absent meaningful limitations that realize a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer or other technical field can show significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that describe a specific application which improves computer functionality or another technical field can amount to significantly more and confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reciting features that improve the computer's basic ability to display information and interact with the user (scaling and relocating text in overlapping windows) or software that controls a device to improve a specific technological process (precision rubber molding) can be eligible because they 'improve another technical field' or 'improve the functioning of the basic display function of the computer itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered-combination analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the ordered combination of claim elements, even if each element is generic, together provides meaningful limitations that amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the totality of steps/elements acting in concert (e.g., constant temperature monitoring + repetitive calculation/comparison + automatic press opening) to determine if they integrate the abstract idea into an improved technological process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data gathering and post-solution activity do not add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere collection of data (e.g., determining a process variable) or post-solution activity (e.g., adjusting an alarm) typically are not sufficient to make a claim significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that only add data gathering or post-solution activity to a formula or algorithm fail Step 2B absent further meaningful integration into a technical process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity fails to add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' do not individually confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim limitations are routine computer functions or conventional activities, the examiner should treat them as not contributing 'significantly more' unless the combination or specific implementation yields a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Step 2B for each abstract idea when multiple are present
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions (e.g., a mathematical relationship and mental steps), the Step 2B analysis must be conducted for each abstract idea separately until ineligibility is shown for one or eligibility is shown for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each abstract-idea thread individually and determine whether additional limitations address that particular exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation affects eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation; if that interpretation covers performance by hand as well as by computer, that fact bears on the abstract-idea analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation covers manual performance of claimed steps, that may support a finding that the claim recites abstract ideas performable mentally or by humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'non-transitory' language to avoid signal coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Including 'non-transitory' in claims can ensure the claim does not encompass transitory signals and helps place a claim in a statutory category (manufacture/article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A non-transitory computer readable medium' ensures the claim is directed to an article, not a signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical transformation or improvement in a technical field supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effect a transformation of a physical article or improve a technical field (e.g., transforming uncured rubber into cured product) can amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical transformation of an article to a different state or thing, or integration of an abstract idea into a process that improves a technological field, are strong indicators of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific application versus mere linking to a technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely linking an abstract idea or formula to a technical field (field-of-use language) without specifying how variables are selected, integrated, or used, does not add significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be meaningful, additional limitations should specify types of variables, how they are selected/gathered, how they are used in the technical process, and how the result is employed to improve the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of mathematical algorithms as judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical formulae and algorithms (including novel ones) are judicial exceptions; novelty of a formula does not by itself remove it from being an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should point to the formula in the claim and explain that it is a mathematical relationship similar to those courts have found abstract (e.g., Arrhenius equation, B1=B0(1.0-F)+PVL(F)).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to frame a rejection or allowance regarding exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection, identify the judicial exception by pointing to the claim elements that recite it and explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. When allowing/clearing, add remarks or reasons for allowance explaining that although the claim recites an exception, the additional limitations—individually or as an ordered combination—demonstrate meaningful improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection should (1) point to the exception (e.g., the formula/mental steps), (2) explain why the preamble does or does not limit the claim, and (3) explain why the additional claim elements fail Step 2B (e.g., mere data gathering, field-of-use, generic computer functions). If eligible, the Office action or reasons for allowance may note that the claim recites the exception but is eligible due to meaningful limitations.
